title: Duke composing the Cotton Club show on the spot and Calloway's lost bet
summary: Duke never wrote introductions or endings down; he gave each man his notes and rhythm at rehearsal, and Cab Calloway lost a bet with Herman Stark that the show would not open on time.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Barney, we were still talking something about Duke.
Yeah, if this heat doesn't get both of us, I mean, we'll be all right.
Yes, it's not the best kind of interviewing weather.

You know, I was thinking, since I saw you last, at the Cotton Club -- you know, Duke used to write a lot of music for the show and it was always a peculiar thing about him, that he'd never make an introduction to the number, whatever, the girls were going to dance, or an ending. So Calloway used to fill the place our place when we'd go on the road from the Cotton Club or the theater or whatever, and he -- there was a manager at the Cotton Club. His name was Herman Stark. The day of the opening of the new show Calloway was betting him that we wouldn't be able to open the show because the music wasn't complete.

So Stark says, 'Well, don't you worry.' He says, 'It'll open and it'll be complete by that time.' So Calloway said, 'No, I bet you.' So they made a wager. And, sure enough, Duke -- we rehearsed that evening and Duke wasn't writing anything down. He'd get on the piano and whatever

rhythm he wanted, he'd give you the rhythm, then he'd give each individual his notes. Now, you had to memorize that, you see. And when he gave everybody their note, then they would start playing it with the rhythm that he wanted, and it came out beautiful. But nobody knew anything about that, the people, you know.
Was everybody in the band able to remember all that all the time?

Yes. Oh, we had to, and if somebody didn't, why, he used to write it down on a piece of empty sheet of music that wasn't anything on it, you know. And he'd just put it up in front of them. You know, after you play it two or three times, well, you knew it. I mean, that was -- and that was the way the ending went.

So Calloway says, "I should go out and shoot myself. That man is phenomenal. He's something else." So Stark said, "I told you." He said, "I never worry about him at all."

I mean, that's the way --
He kind of liked deadlines and doing things the last minute.
